Our tests provide strong evidence for Part 1 - that males and females penguins differ significantly in size within each species. We examined individual measurements (t-tests), all measurements considered together (Hotelling's T²) and the covariance structure (Box's M), which showed that not only do the average measurements differ by sex, but the way the measurements relate to one another. For covariance structure, Adelie differed from the other species. While the means for Adelie had a significant difference, its covariance shape did not differ significantly between sexes (p = 0.061), suggesting Adelie males and females vary in a more similar way than for males and females of Gentoo or Chinstrap species.
 
Our analysis also shows in Part 2 that sex has a visible and clear effect on species classification. In the model without distinction for sex, penguins 68, 124, 286, and 296 were misclassified; however, in the model with sex considered, these individuals are no longer misclassified - although penguin 274 then becomes misclassified.

Adelie males ID 68 and ID 124 seems to have longer bill length and flipper length. Based on the 3 centroids of Adelie, Gentoo and Chinstrap in the first model, these individuals seem to be larger and closer to the Chinstrap centroid and further from the Adelie centroid due to inclusion of Adelie females which bring averages down. However, once we factor in sex into the model, and split each species off by sex, these individuals are closest to Adelie male due to resulting more accurate mean measurements.

In the original model, Chinstrap female 286 and 296 are misclassified as Adelie until sex is considered. This is the opposite to our previous example. 286 and 296 seems to have shorter bill lengths and shorter flipper lengths. In addition, 296 seems to have a lower body mass and shorter bill_depth. In the model with consideration for within-species sex, we can see these individuals now appear closer to Chinstrap females.


Misclassification with our second model suggest that penguin ID 274 is a Chinstrap female that falls into the general range of chinstrap based on measurements when no sex considered. However, once sex is factored in, the measurements of penguin 274 lies closer to Adelie-male centroid. 

We note a limitation of this analysis as classification was performed using the same limited sample data set, and therefore, our results may not be consistent with results from a new sample of the population.

We also note that we did not run the model for the 11 penguins with unconfirmed sex (dropped at the start from the dataset). However, this could be a future direction to determine whether sex can be determined based on measurements when sex is unknown.
